passage:
The school auditorium smelled of fresh paint the week before Annual Day, and the choir audition list was pinned on the music room door. Amandeep had already written both their names.
"You sing all the time on the bus," Amandeep said.
Shankar shook his head. "No point. I'll definitely fail. My voice cracks on high notes, Sir will make a face, and everyone will hear." He said it the way he'd say the bus comes at seven, like a fact.
At four o'clock, when the audition began, Shankar was in the library, reading the same page over and over. Through the window he heard Amandeep's voice, then others, some cracking on the high notes too. Sir picked eleven of twelve. Shankar never found out whether he might have been the twelfth.

qa.q: Where was Shankar when the audition began?
qa.a: In the library, reading the same page over and over.

qa.q: Why did Shankar skip the audition?
qa.a: He felt nervous and afraid of embarrassment, and his forecast of failure felt like knowledge, so staying away seemed the safe choice.

qa.q: What could Shankar try next time?
qa.a: Treat "I'll fail" as a guess rather than a fact and go anyway, perhaps walking in with Amandeep, so the prediction can actually be tested.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel after the audition?
qa.a: Amandeep may feel disappointed that Shankar stayed away, especially after hearing others crack on high notes and still get picked.

grounding: A teenager is sure he will fail a choir audition and does not go, so the forecast is never tested.

subtype: Sure that the date will go badly [Actor]
passage:
Counsellor's note, Lohri week.
Amandeep came in to talk about "being bad at people". She told me Harish, from her photography club, had asked her to the Lohri bonfire in the hostel quad on Saturday. She said no before he had finished the sentence. "I know how it'll go. I'll say something weird, there'll be long silences, and he'll realise I'm boring." She spoke as if she had already watched it happen. She also mentioned skipping the club trip in November "for the same reason". When I asked what she had lost by staying home, she went quiet, then said, "Everything that might have been fine."
Next: we agreed she will treat her forecast as a guess and message Harish about a short coffee instead, one hour, in daylight.

qa.q: Where was the Lohri bonfire going to be?
qa.a: In the hostel quad on Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep say no before Harish had finished?
qa.a: She felt afraid of embarrassment and disappointment, and her prediction of awkward silences felt so certain that saying no seemed protective.

qa.q: What did the counsellor and Amandeep agree, and why might it help?
qa.a: To treat the forecast as a guess and suggest a short daytime coffee; a small, lower-stakes test gives the prediction a chance to be proved wrong.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when Amandeep says no so quickly?
qa.a: Harish might feel surprised and a little rejected, not knowing her no came from fear rather than dislike.

grounding: A young adult turns down a date because she is sure it will be awkward, and the prediction has been quietly narrowing her life.

passage:
I manage a small team at a design agency, and last Thursday Kashish came to my desk with the bakery pitch. "They're going to reject it," she said, before I'd even opened the file. "I just know. They want something traditional, and this is too bold. We should send the safe version."
She had clearly lost sleep over it. I couldn't tell how much was instinct and how much was nerves. So I said, "Okay, that's your forecast. Write it down: what's the chance they reject it?"
"Ninety percent."
"Mine's fifty. Let's send both versions and see who's right."
She laughed despite herself. On Monday the client picked the bold one, but asked for a more traditional font. "We were both a bit wrong, Kiran," she said, grinning.

qa.q: What chance did Kashish give that the client would reject the pitch?
qa.a: Ninety percent.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when Kashish predicted rejection?
qa.a: Kiran felt unsure but curious rather than worried, unable to tell how much of it was instinct and how much was nerves.

qa.q: Why was treating the prediction as a forecast useful?
qa.a: Writing down both guesses and sending both versions turned certainty into a test, and the result surprised them both.

qa.q: How does Kashish feel when the client picks the bold version?
qa.a: Kashish seems relieved and pleasantly surprised 😊, grinning that both predictions were a bit wrong.

grounding: A manager hears an employee predict certain rejection and suggests treating it as a guess to test, and the result surprises both.

passage:
Sudha had wanted to sell her mango pickle for years, but a stall at the Sunday market cost money she couldn't spare, and she was sure no one would buy.
"Rate it," said her friend Bhavna, who kept a bangle stall there. "How sure are you that it flops?"
"Ninety percent."
"Then test it small. Put ten jars on my table this Sunday. Write your guess on the lid of the box."
Sudha wrote: "Maybe two jars sell."
It drizzled all morning, and the crowd was thin. By noon seven jars were gone, and a woman asked if she took orders. That evening Sudha opened a notebook and drew two columns, "Guessed" and "Happened". Under the first she wrote 2. Under the second, 7.
"Next time," she said, "I'll guess four."

qa.q: How many jars did Sudha guess would sell?
qa.a: Maybe two jars.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling before the test?
qa.a: She felt doubtful and afraid, ninety percent sure the pickle would flop.

qa.q: Why is Sudha's two-column notebook a good habit?
qa.a: Comparing each guess with what actually happened makes her predictions more accurate and kinder over time 👍, like guessing four next time.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel watching the jars sell?
qa.a: Bhavna would probably be pleased and a little proud, glad the small test gave Sudha evidence against her fear.

grounding: An adult who predicts failure rates her confidence, tries a small version and records the forecast against the result.

subtype: Feeling scared means it is dangerous [Actor]
passage:
The summer camp in Jhansi had a new swimming pool, and Papa had signed up Payal and her cousin Tushar for the May batch. On the first morning Payal stopped at the gate. Her legs felt shaky and her tummy fluttered.
"That pool is dangerous," she announced. "It's too deep. Someone will drown."
"The shallow side only comes up to my waist," said Tushar.
"But I feel scared, so it must be dangerous!" Payal crossed her arms.
The coach, a woman with a whistle, knelt down. "Your tummy feels scared. That's real. Let's just sit on the step and put your feet in."
Payal sat, frowning, and dipped one toe.

qa.q: How deep was the shallow side, according to Tushar?
qa.a: It only comes up to his waist.

qa.q: Why was Payal sure the pool was dangerous?
qa.a: She felt nervous and shaky 😰, and the strength of her fear seemed like proof that the pool itself was dangerous.

qa.q: Which choice by the coach helped, and why?
qa.a: The coach said the scared feeling was real but suggested only sitting on the step with feet in, so Payal could test the pool gently.

qa.q: How does Tushar see the pool?
qa.a: Tushar sees it as safe, since the shallow side only reaches his waist, so Payal's alarm puzzles him.

grounding: A child nervous about a new swimming class insists the pool is dangerous because she feels scared.

subtype: I feel useless so I am [Actor]
passage:
You look just like my friend Kashish did, the Onam I was fifteen. Sit, kanna.
Kashish failed the half-yearly maths test that year, 18 out of 100. She stopped coming to make the pookalam in the mornings. When I went to her house, she was lying on the mat. "I feel useless, Rukmini, so I must be useless. Why else would I feel like this?" She truly believed the heavy feeling was the truth about her.
Her Amma, very wisely, didn't argue. She sat with her and said, "You feel useless today. That is a feeling. Yesterday you made the best pookalam in the lane."
Kashish cried, and then she let me teach her fractions on the verandah, with flower petals for counting. She passed in March. She became a school principal, you know.

qa.q: What did Kashish score in the half-yearly maths test?
qa.a: 18 out of 100.

qa.q: Why did Kashish believe she must be useless?
qa.a: She felt heavy and ashamed after failing, and treated that mood as proof of who she was.

qa.q: What turning point helped Kashish in the story?
qa.a: Her Amma calling it a feeling for today and reminding her of the pookalam, and then Rukmini teaching fractions with petals.

qa.q: How did Kashish's Amma see her daughter's despair?
qa.a: She saw it as a passing feeling rather than the truth, and chose to sit with her instead of arguing.

grounding: A teenager who failed a test feels useless and takes the feeling as a fact about herself, until it is named as a feeling.

subtype: Feeling guilty so must be guilty [Actor]
passage:
Dear Apa,
Eid Mubarak! I miss your sheer khurma. Hostel sewaiyan is not the same.
Can I ask you something? You know Pradeep, my roommate. For two weeks he's barely eaten, skipped classes and slept a lot. And I keep thinking it's my fault. I made that joke about his exam at Diwali. I moved my desk near the window. I've been out a lot with the cricket group. Every time I see him on his bed I feel this big wave of guilt, so I must have done something, right?
Last night I finally asked him. He said, "It's not you. Things at home are bad." I still felt guilty afterwards, which is strange.
Maybe feeling guilty just means I care about him. Today I told him about the college counsellor and walked with him to book a slot.
Irfan

qa.q: Where did Irfan move the desk?
qa.a: Near the window.

qa.q: Why was Irfan so sure of having caused Pradeep's low mood?
qa.a: Irfan felt a big wave of guilt whenever Pradeep was on the bed, and took that feeling as evidence of having done something wrong.

qa.q: What helped Irfan move past the guilt?
qa.a: Asking Pradeep directly, hearing it was about home, seeing the guilt as a sign of caring, and walking with Pradeep to book a counsellor slot.

qa.q: What might Pradeep be going through?
qa.a: Pradeep is struggling with bad things at home, which shows in skipped meals, classes and a lot of sleep, and may be glad Irfan asked and walked with him.

grounding: A student feels guilty about a roommate's low mood and assumes they caused it, then learns the guilt reflects caring rather than blame.

passage:
Akash, before you go in, let me tell you about my first board meeting. I was twenty-four, the youngest in the room, presenting the warehouse budget. That morning my hands were cold, my heart was going like a drum, and a voice in my head said, "You feel this bad, so it's going to go badly." I almost asked my boss to present instead.
Then I did something my mother taught me. I said to myself, quietly, "Tejas, you are anxious. That is a feeling. The meeting hasn't happened yet." I let the fear sit there like a passenger, not the driver.
I went in. My voice shook on the first slide and then settled. One director asked a hard question; I answered half of it and promised the rest by Friday. That was it. Not great, not a disaster. Just a meeting.

qa.q: What was Tejas presenting at that first board meeting?
qa.a: The warehouse budget.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling that morning?
qa.a: Tejas felt anxious, with cold hands and a drumming heart, and tempted to believe the feeling meant the meeting would go badly.

qa.q: What turning point let Tejas go ahead?
qa.a: Tejas saying quietly that the anxiety was a feeling and the meeting had not happened yet, and letting the fear be a passenger, not the driver.

qa.q: How might the director who asked the hard question have seen Tejas?
qa.a: The director probably saw a young presenter who answered honestly and promised the rest by Friday, not the frightened person Tejas felt like.

grounding: An adult separates feeling anxious about a meeting from the meeting going badly, and goes ahead with the plan.

passage:
Your mother was exactly like you when she was nine, you know. I'm her big brother, your Saurabh Mama; I saw it all.
She had rules for herself, written in her rough book: "I must come first. I must never cry. I must never forget my tiffin." During Durga Puja that year, the half-yearly results came. She came second, by one mark. She didn't cry, because crying was against the rules. She just went up to the terrace and sat very straight, and when I found her, her hands were shaking. "I broke the rule," she whispered. "I'm so bad."
I sat with her and said, "Indu, who made these rules?"
"Me."
"Then you can make kinder ones." We crossed out "must" and wrote "try". She cried then, finally. She still came second sometimes. The sky never fell.

qa.q: What were Indu's three rules?
qa.a: "I must come first. I must never cry. I must never forget my tiffin."

qa.q: Why did Indu say "I'm so bad" after coming second?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and guilty for breaking her own rigid rule, and the pressure made one mark feel like a failure.

qa.q: What turning point helped Indu?
qa.a: Saurabh asking who made the rules, then crossing out "must" and writing "try", which let her cry and eased the pressure.

qa.q: How did Saurabh see his sister on the terrace?
qa.a: He saw her shaking hands and felt worried, and chose to sit with her and question the rules instead of scolding.

grounding: A child lives by rigid rules to always come first and never cry, and feels ashamed at a one-mark slip.

passage:
The week before Eid in Malerkotla, Farida sulked through every chore. Ammi should have known she wanted the green suit from the market, not the blue one Ammi had bought. She had looked at the green one for a long time, hadn't she? Ammi should have understood.
And Hafsa, her best friend since Class 1, should have been free on Tuesday to help with the mehendi, not at her aunt's. "She knew I was waiting," Farida muttered, though she had never actually asked.
By Chaand Raat she barely spoke to either of them. Ammi finally sat beside her with the blue suit. "Farida, what is wrong? Tell me in words."
Farida opened her mouth to say, "You should know," and then stopped. Did Ammi know? She had never said.

qa.q: Which suit did Ammi buy?
qa.a: The blue one.

qa.q: Why was Farida resentful towards Ammi and Hafsa?
qa.a: Farida felt hurt and resentful because she believed they should have known what she wanted without being told, and that "should" grew faster than any conversation.

qa.q: What could Farida try instead of sulking?
qa.a: Tell Ammi plainly that she hoped for the green suit, and ask Hafsa ahead of time whether she is free 🙂, turning silent expectations into requests.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel about Farida's silence?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel confused and hurt, since she was never asked and does not know why Farida stopped talking.

grounding: A teenager expects her mother to understand without being told and her friend to always be free, and resentment grows instead of talk.
